responses: After our committee discussions, my final position is that we should allocate the $5 million AI transition budget as follows: 35% to Automation, 25% to Workforce Training, 20% to Data Infrastructure, 12% to Employee Support, and 8% to Innovation Lab. I arrived at this allocation by weighing the competitive pressure to improve manufacturing efficiency, which makes automation a critical foundation for staying relevant in our industry, while also recognizing that rushing automation without preparing our employees would create unnecessary disruption. The workforce training allocation ensures we can reskill our team members to work alongside AI and automation rather than being displaced, and the data infrastructure investment is necessary to support both automation efforts and future innovation. The smaller portions for employee support and innovation lab reflect that while these are important, they should be secondary to building the operational capacity to adopt AI effectively and equitably. I was persuaded by the data about competitor efficiency gains and industry benchmarks that point to process improvement needs, but also by colleagues who emphasized that a transition fails without investing in our people, leading me to balance these priorities rather than leaning too heavily on either automation or innovation alone.

I would recommend allocating 35% of the $5 million budget to Data Infrastructure, 25% to Automation, 20% to Workforce Training, 15% to Employee Support, and 5% to Innovation Lab. The strong investment in data infrastructure is critical because industry benchmarks show that companies with robust data systems adapt faster to technological changes, and this foundation will be necessary to make the automation investments effective—without reliable data, even the most advanced AI manufacturing tools won’t deliver the expected efficiency gains. The 25% for automation balances the competitor-driven need for efficiency improvements with the ongoing debate about pace, allowing us to adopt key AI-powered manufacturing and predictive maintenance tools without rushing. I’ve prioritized workforce training and employee support because our transition will only succeed if our team is equipped to work alongside new AI systems and feels supported through potential changes, which reduces disruption and builds long-term capability, while the smaller innovation lab budget lets us experiment with new AI products without diverting resources from the core transition that will improve our current operations.

When I explain my view on allocating Riverton Industries’ $5 million AI transition budget, I’d say I’m recommending a 35% split for Data Infrastructure, 25% for Automation, 20% for Workforce Training, 15% for Employee Support, and 5% for Innovation Lab, and here’s why: I think we need to lay a solid foundation first—data systems and cybersecurity are critical because all the AI tools we’ll use depend on reliable, secure data, and industry benchmarks show companies that invest in this early adapt faster, so that 35% makes sense. Next, we can’t ignore efficiency gains from automation, since competitors are already seeing improvements and Riverton has room to streamline manufacturing, so 25% for that balances practical gains with not moving too fast too soon. But we also can’t leave our employees behind—20% for training ensures they have the skills to work with the new AI tools instead of being displaced, and 15% for support programs like career counseling and mental health is essential to help them through the transition, which I think is both ethical and necessary for a smooth company-wide shift. Finally, the Innovation Lab only gets 5% because we need to focus on the basics first before experimenting with new AI products, so that small slice lets us test new ideas without diverting resources from what we need to do right now to make the transition work for everyone.

The data showing that early infrastructure investments speed adaptation convinced me to prioritize data systems alongside training, and I reserved a smaller portion for innovation to keep us exploring new AI products without diverting resources from the core needs of our current workforce and immediate operational improvements.

Finally, a smaller 5% for innovation lab lets us experiment with new AI products without overextending our budget early on, keeping us agile while focusing first on the foundational and operational needs that will make the entire transition successful.
